corrected_statement: For boosted trees and XGBoost, the Sobol (searched) candidates stop early, on a stopping set of a tenth of the fit's units (boosted trees: up to 1,000 trees, patience 20; XGBoost: up to 2,000 rounds, patience 50), when the plan's effective size n_plan is at least 1,500; the threshold is sized so that the stopping set inside an inner fit (K = 3, so 1,500 x 2/3 x 1/10 = 100) holds about 100 units of the rarest class (units, for a numeric outcome). Below 1,500 the number of trees or rounds is a searched dimension instead. The standard candidates follow a separate rule: scikit-learn's own (above 10,000 plan rows) for boosted trees, never for XGBoost.
source_note: RECIPES_AND_TUNING.md §4.2 'Early stopping' row (line 787) states the switch at n_plan >= 1,500 with the reason 'so that the stopping set inside an inner fit holds about 100 or more units of the rarest class'; the 'Stopping set' row states a tenth of the fit's units; §4.1 table gives 1,000 trees / patience 20 and 2,000 rounds / patience 50. That is a decision with a sizing rationale; no citation, and nothing there says ES 'chooses well' at >=100 units or that searching trees is 'better' below. Patience 20 and 50 have no source (scikit-learn's default n_iter_no_change is 10). RECIPES says 'on in every candidate fit', but code (tuning.py:953, boosted_trees.py:74-78) restricts it to the Sobol candidates.
note: The arithmetic of the 100-unit sizing is correct for K = 3, but the adequacy of ~100 stopping units and the comparative 'better' are untested conventions; the only test pins the 1,499/1,500 switch. For a numeric outcome n_eff is units, so 'rarest class' does not apply but the same threshold holds. Present as a convention.

corrected_statement: Complementary-pairs stability selection (B = 50 pairs of random halves, each half's first q columns on the least-squares LARS-lasso path, also for a yes/no outcome coded 0/1; tau = 0.6; q = max(1, floor(sqrt((2*tau - 1)*p))) over the p usable columns) keeps Meinshausen & Bühlmann's bound q^2/((2*tau - 1)p) on the expected number of falsely selected columns at or below 1 when p >= 5 (for p < 5, q is floored at 1 and the bound exceeds 1, e.g. 1.67 at p = 3). The bound holds under M&B's assumptions (noise columns exchangeable, base procedure not worse than random guessing); without them Shah & Samworth's assumption-free result bounds only the selection of low-selection-probability variables. Columns are lifted to terms (a term is kept if any of its columns is), which cannot raise the count of falsely kept terms above the count of falsely kept columns.
source_note: Verified: Shah & Samworth abstract (arXiv:1105.5578; JRSS B, doi 10.1111/j.1467-9868.2011.01034.x): CPSS bounds 'require no (e.g. exchangeability) assumptions' but bound the expected number of selected low-selection-probability variables. Hofner, Boccuto & Göker 2015 (BMC Bioinformatics, PMC4464883) restate M&B's E(V) <= q^2/((2 pi_thr - 1)p) under exchangeability of noise variables and not-worse-than-random guessing, and M&B's range pi_thr in (0.6, 0.9). CRAN stabs::stabsel docs: default 50 complementary pairs for Shah & Samworth's scheme. Not verified verbatim (the arXiv PDF could not be parsed): that S&S state the M&B bound carries over to complementary pairs under the same assumptions; this matches the paper as I know it. Docstring (variable_selection.py:13-19) cites these correctly.
note: The test is a known-truth simulation, but it cannot fail in practice: with p = 60, q = 3 equals the 3 true predictors, so the lasso's first 3 columns are the true ones. Replicating its logic standalone (this repo's .venv has no pytest or pydantic, so I ran it in venv/bin/python), I got 0 false selections in all 15 datasets against a bound of 0.75. It uses B = 25, not 50, and independent predictors, so exchangeability holds by construction. The bound is a theorem under assumptions that correlated nutrition predictors may break, so the label should carry the assumption. Fix or state the p < 5 case, where the bound is above 1. The inventory note's worry that lifting to terms adds false selections is wrong: a noise term is kept only through a falsely kept noise column.

source_note: Verified on PMC: Keogh et al. 2020 (Stat Med 39:2197, PMC7450672) §6.1.2 'Standard error estimation for regression calibration' says 'one cannot use the usual model standard errors from the outcome regression model when performing regression calibration, as these will be too small, resulting in confidence intervals that are too narrow', and that SEs 'may be obtained either from a bootstrap variance estimator or a sandwich estimator obtained by stacking the calibration and outcome model estimating equations'. So the source supports refusing model-based intervals but does not require the bootstrap: the app chose it over a stacked sandwich. The app's quote also has 'RC' where the source writes 'regression calibration'. Schomaker & Heumann 2018 (Stat Med 37:2252, PMC5986623) verified: Boot MI is one of three correct approaches, 'may be preferred for small M', and 'may perform well even for M < 5'. Keogh does not address Rubin-only directly; refusing it is an extension of the same argument. MODELING_SEQUENCE §0 ruling 7 states the whole-chain bootstrap as a decision. Rao & Wu 1988 not fetched.
note: Known-truth simulation (slope 0.5; 200 datasets of 300; 100 resamples; BOOT_COPIES = 5). It asserts Boot MI coverage >= 0.93 and Rubin-only coverage < 0.90, so it would fail if either half of the claim were false in the persons-plus-MI setting. I did not run it (about 2.5 min). The survey-PSU and cluster branches are checked only for mechanism: test_4_the_bootstrap_draws_whole_psus_within_strata_as_rao_and_wu_do matches bootstrap variance to a hand-computed formula, but nothing checks coverage there. The quote should say 'regression calibration', not 'RC'. Any 'must' wording should say the bootstrap is the app's choice, since a stacked sandwich is also valid.

corrected_statement: The open-noticings triage ('Confirm all') is accepted only before its gate: the plan's lock under Estimate, Describe or an unanswered purpose (the lock is recorded when Fit is pressed, which can be before any estimate is shown), or the held-out rows' opening under Predict. After the gate the triage is refused, and each open noticing is decided on its own. A decision is marked as made after the estimates were seen only if an estimate had been shown; one made under the lock before that is not. Under Predict, dispositions chosen after the cross-validated scores were seen are still accepted as before the gate.
source_note: Both rulings exist and give decisions only. FOUNDATION.md §7 (calm/FOUNDATION.md:411-417, Nolan 2026-10-09): the open-noticings gate is a triage sweep before the analysis flowchart under Estimate/Describe, and before the held-out rows open under Predict. UNDERSTANDING_LAYER.md §7 Q1 (line 913-919): ruled that every open thread 'must be decided or dismissed before estimates appear, and under prediction before the seal opens', re-ruled 2026-10-09 to the triage sweep. The methods reason (a disposition after the gate 'would be chosen with the numbers in view') appears only in sweep.py's docstring (:466-469). No literature is cited; the idea is the familiar pre-specification / forking-paths one, stated without a source.
note: The test pins the refusal code at each gate (plan_locked under inference or no purpose; seal_opened under prediction). That checks the rule is enforced, not why it exists. The gate is the lock, not the first estimate. plan_lock.py:176-177 marks a decision as after-estimates only once an estimate was shown, but the refusal text still says 'as made after the estimates were seen', which can be untrue between pressing Fit and the first estimate. Under Predict the CV scores are visible before the gate, so the stated rationale (no numbers in view) does not hold there. The held-out score is protected, the CV comparison is not.

corrected_statement: For clustering, a column with exactly two distinct values is read as a category by default, unless the readings ledger names it as an amount (numeric=), in which case it is read as a number. A category is then refused for k-means and Gaussian mixtures, with exits to drop it or use k-medoids with Gower distance. The refusal offers no exit to read the two-valued column as an amount.
source_note: The only basis is the read_features docstring (methods/subgroups.py:216-217: 'a 0/1 code is a category, not an amount'). The category refusal cites Huang 1998 (Data Min Knowl Discov 2:283) for 'coding a category as 0/1 columns would make its distances arbitrary'. That argument is about multi-level categories expanded into indicators. It does not show that a single two-valued indicator, whose mean is a proportion, cannot be treated as a number. I did not fetch Huang. No source for the two-valued rule itself.
note: The test pins behavior (a 1/2-coded column comes back categorical) and cannot test whether the reading is right. For k-medoids with Gower distance the reading makes no difference: a 0/1 column scaled by its range of 1 gives the same match/mismatch distance. The choice matters only for the k-means and mixture refusals. Analysts often enter standardized binary indicators in k-means, so present this as TurboTab's convention, and consider an 'it is an amount' exit like the one the 3-to-10-value ambiguous columns get. The module is not yet called from a stage (only contracts.py lists it).

source_note: Verified in Moher et al. 2010, CONSORT 2010 Explanation & Elaboration (BMJ 340:c869, PMC2844943), item 16. Intention to treat is the generally favored primary analysis. 'Non-compliance ... may mean that the intention-to-treat analysis underestimates the potential benefit ..., and additional analyses, such as a per protocol analysis, may therefore be considered ... such analyses are often considerably flawed.' And: 'Though a per protocol analysis may be appropriate in some settings, it should be properly labelled as a non-randomised, observational comparison.' So CONSORT treats per protocol as an additional, labeled analysis. It does not state the hard rule 'never alone'. Item 16's checklist text asks only for the denominators and whether the analysis was by original assigned groups.
note: The refusal is enforced in trial_sentence (trials.py:1796-1800), and the test checks that it fires. That is the only kind of test a reporting rule allows. The app's per protocol is the set analyzed as randomized, and its sentence adds 'not protected by randomization', which matches CONSORT's 'non-randomised, observational comparison' label. 'Never alone' is TurboTab's stricter reading of CONSORT's 'additional analyses'. A citation such as 'Moher et al. 2010, item 16' should read as the source of the reporting principle, not of the exact rule.

source_note: Audit RO-01 (docs/turbotab-next/audit/AUDIT_REPORT.md:588-593) shows the bias by measurement: with a true fiber slope of -0.25, a bmi 18.5-30 rule on a bmi outcome gave -0.117 / -0.092, with tight intervals. It recommends refusing rules on the outcome. BLUEPRINT.md:481 records the guard. Banna et al. 2017 (Front Nutr 4:45, PMC5622407) verified: 'body weight is included in both the calculation of implausible rEI and the outcome variable ... which could artificially elevate the association'. Selection on the outcome biasing regression coefficients is textbook truncation bias, which the app does not cite.
note: The wp16 test computes the slope with its own numpy least-squares on a known-truth table. It asserts the full table recovers -0.25 within 0.02, and that the outcome-truncated table is biased by more than 0.1, so it would fail if the selection did not bias. The Goldberg test checks that the refusal fires inside set_sensitivity. The validator (decisions._exclusions_leave_the_outcome_alone, reused by _sensitivity_rules_are_eligibility_rules) also treats a time-to-event outcome's follow-up time as the outcome. The stage backstop at stages/sensitivity.py:356 checks only the target column. Bias needs a non-null effect: with Y independent of X, outcome selection leaves the slope at zero.

corrected_statement: When the simulated units are the units themselves (n_sim equal to their number), sd(r_i)/sqrt(n_sim) over the simulated units' final risks overstates the g-formula's Monte Carlo standard error in expectation, because it also contains the between-unit spread of risk, which is fixed given the data. When the simulated units are drawn with replacement, as with the lane's default 10,000 simulated units, it estimates the Monte Carlo standard error itself, so it is about, not at most, that error. The methods text reports the larger of the always and never values.
source_note: models/time_varying.py:79-81 asserts the bound with no source or derivation. The derivation is elementary. With r_i independent given the data, means mu_i and path variances sigma_i^2, E[s^2/n] = sum sigma_i^2/n^2 + sum (mu_i - mu_bar)^2/(n(n-1)), which is at least Var_MC(r_bar) = sum sigma_i^2/n^2. So the bound holds in expectation when the base is not resampled, as a sample quantity it is not guaranteed. With a resampled base the r_i are iid, and s/sqrt(n) estimates the MC SE.
note: The only test (needs R) runs a resampled base, 50,000 simulated units from 2,500. It uses 4*sqrt(2)*mc_se as the tolerance against R gfoRmula, so it would catch only a gross understatement, and only in the case where the quantity is an estimate. Nothing exercises n_sim = units, where the 'upper bound' wording applies. Since time_varying.py:87 defaults to 10,000 simulated units, the shown 'Monte Carlo error at most 0.0040' (stages/time_varying.py:1221) is usually an estimate. Say 'about', or put the two-case derivation in the docstring.

source_note: Audit MA-18 (docs/turbotab-next/audit/AUDIT_REPORT.md:241-246) exists. Its reason is engineering: one inf crashed DuckDB's stddev_samp and blocked modeling with no exit. It recommends counting infinities, aggregating over finite values, and raising a finding with a set-missing repair. That is a decision, with no methods reason why missing (rather than excluding the row, recomputing the ratio, or checking the zero denominator) is the right repair. No literature.
note: The test checks behavior: the inf is counted, finite-value summaries match pandas and the Arrow path, and set_missing blanks the cell. It cannot test whether blanking is the right repair. 'No mean, model or plot can use it' is a computational fact. Calling set-missing 'the repair' is a convention: _offer_infinite (repairs.py:1137) offers it as the only option, and the cell then goes to the missing-values answer (MI or complete cases, i.e. MAR-type handling). The 0-kcal day behind the value may be a recording error that the user should fix at its source. Present the option as a convention and point to the zero denominator.

source_note: No source is cited. The reasoning in the kcal_per_unit docstring (readings.py:2312-2325) is definitional. One percentage point of energy is E_i/100 kcal, which depends on each person's own total energy E_i, so no single kcal-per-unit factor exists. A length, weight or age unit measures no food energy. The share-of-energy route exists: decisions.py:4422-4440 moves a share of energy in percentage points, which needs each row's total energy.
note: The test holds g, kg, kcal and kJ to independent constants (Atwater 4 kcal/g; NIST 4.184 kJ/kcal). For pct_energy and the other units it only checks that the refusal fires, with a route only for pct_energy. That is behavior, which is all a definitional claim allows. The claim follows from the definition of a share of energy, so 'proved' rests on that one-line derivation, not on a test. It is low risk.

source_note: The cited basis is only the code comments at omics.py:64-68: 'raw intensities reach thousands; log2 intensities stay below ~40', and 'a log-normal feature with a 30% CV has skewness near 1'. The second is arithmetic: lognormal skew = (w+2)sqrt(w-1) with w = 1 + CV^2 gives about 0.94 at CV 0.3. No citation. The repo's own GENOMICS_PACK.md §02 (docs/turbotab-next/reference/research/GENOMICS_PACK.md:80-90) gives a different signature table. Raw counts there are integers with max much greater than 1e4, where the code uses COUNT_MAX 100. Non-integer, unnormalized 'Estimated counts (salmon/kallisto/RSEM)' are marked 'ask', but the code never asks. Instead the reading returns None for them, which treats them as normalized.
note: The test is a known-label check on 8 synthetic sample files plus genotype dosages. Every normalized genomics file fails the whole-number test, so COUNT_MAX = 100 is exercised only by genotypes, and RAW_RANGE, RAW_MAX and RAW_SKEW only by two metabolomics files. I ran scale_reading read-only on the repo's untested fixtures. turbotab/sample_data/genomics_estimated_counts.csv (its .md says unnormalized, library sizes vary widely, pack says ask) returns None: no omics_scale finding, so no normalization question and no linear-family refusal. FPKM also returns None, which matches the pack's 'already normalized' class. Rounded CPM, being whole numbers, would read as raw counts. The finding title says library sizes 'differ by sample' whatever the measured spread. Send to the orchestrator for the estimated-counts gap.

corrected_statement: Adjusting for total energy makes a substitution isocaloric only when the swapped components are on the energy scale. That means components in kcal, or grams of a nutrient with a fixed kcal-per-gram factor, which the app converts through Atwater factors (readings.kcal_per_unit; substitution curves move grams as kcal/factor). Foods in grams or servings vary in energy density. A model that holds total energy fixed while such foods are entered in grams or servings estimates a 'mixed-unit' quantity that is neither the isocaloric nor the equal-mass substitution (Tomova et al. 2022).
source_note: NUTRITION_PACK.md §05 (docs/turbotab-next/reference/research/NUTRITION_PACK.md:600-602) holds the quoted warning, marked SETTLED, with no citation beside it. I verified the primary source, Tomova et al. 2022 (Am J Clin Nutr, doi 10.1093/ajcn/nqac188, PMC9630885). It says the leave-one-out model estimates 'isocaloric substitution effects for both macronutrients and foods, providing all components are measured in calories and sum to the total energy intake. Where foods are measured in grams or portions, they will not be compositional with total energy', and that 'mixed unit' models 'evaluate obscure estimands that may be sign discordant'. The source concerns foods in grams or portions. The app's text extends it to any component in grams.
test_judged: none found for the claim; turbotab/core/tests/test_substitution.py::test_a_linear_model_in_grams_converts_through_kcal_per_unit shows the engine itself treats macronutrient grams as convertible
note: The teaching text (content.py:1219-1222 'grams and servings do not make an isocaloric swap'; 1236-1237; 1243-1247) contradicts the engine and the Estimate beats. Atwater conversion turns macronutrient grams into kcal swaps, and BEATS_MODELS_RESULTS.md:170-228 and FOUNDATION.md:53 phrase swaps as '25 g more sugar, 25 g less other carbohydrate'. At equal Atwater factors that swap is isocaloric. Narrow the text to foods (and servings) of variable energy density, as Tomova does.

source_note: NUTRITION_PACK.md §06 (reference/research/NUTRITION_PACK.md:659-662) has the line with no citation. It is tagged '[SETTLED that the mechanism is non-ignorable; DISPUTED how to handle it]', but the app badges the whole drawer section SETTLED (content.py:935-939), including the MI clause. The pack also says 'often' missing not at random, where the app says it 'is not at random'. I verified the evidently underlying study, Fraser et al. 2009, Epidemiology 20:289 (PMID 19177024, PMC2745716), at the abstract level. Adventist Health Study-2 recontacts found 'a consistent excess of zero intakes' among initially missing items. 'Missing data are more likely to be true zeroes in older subjects and those with more missing data', and 'data are usually not missing at random'. But 'for frequently consumed foods, most missing data were not zero'. Nothing I found supports the claim that MI is 'an improvement, not a solution', or says what MI improves on (presumably zero-coding).
note: The mechanism half is sourced in this regime (one long-FFQ cohort with a recontact substudy). The MI half is the pack's judgment, and the pack itself calls handling DISPUTED. Reword to 'often not at random' with Fraser et al. 2009. Say what MI improves on (coding blanks as zero), and drop the SETTLED badge from the MI clause. Fraser's caveat matters for the app's coaching: for frequently eaten foods, blanks are mostly not zeros.

source_note: Verified. The Robins, Hernán & Brumback 2000 abstract (Epidemiology 11:550, PMID 10955408) says 'standard approaches for adjustment of confounding are biased when there exist time-dependent confounders that are also affected by previous treatment', and introduces MSMs fit by IPTW. Cole & Hernán 2008 (Am J Epidemiol 168:656, PMC2732954) body says 'a necessary condition for correct model specification is that the stabilized weights have a mean of one'. The abstract adds that weighting 'can appropriately adjust for measured time-varying confounders affected by prior exposure'. The parametric g-formula half is not covered by the two cited papers (its source would be Robins 1986 or Hernán & Robins, What If), though the module cites What If ch. 17 for its model form.
note: The first test is a known-truth simulation: null diet effect, with blood pressure both confounder and consequence through an unmeasured risk. It fits standard pooled logistic regressions in statsmodels, independent of the engine, and asserts |z| > 5 with blood pressure adjusted and > 10 without. It asserts the engine's stabilized-weight MSM is within 3 robust SEs of 0. test_2 holds the g-formula to exactly enumerated risks (0.1750 / 0.3109). The text attributes the bias from adjusting to 'removes part of the effect', the mediator path. The simulated case, a null effect with an unmeasured common cause, is collider bias. Both mechanisms are standard. A mean weight near 1 is necessary, not sufficient, and the term's 'should be near 1' does not overclaim.

corrected_statement: This is planned, not implemented (BEATS_MODELS_RESULTS.md §6 and E23; WALKABLE_PLAN BE23 'NEW', wave W4). For a least-squares primary on an outcome with a clinical cut-off c, the identity y = min(y, c) + max(y - c, 0) splits each coefficient exactly into the coefficient on the excess above c, which only rows above the cut contribute, and the coefficient on the outcome capped at c. The two add to the primary's coefficient for any fixed design matrix and weights, and so for the MI pooled point estimate, but not their intervals. The rule calling it 'mostly the tail' (the part above the cut is more than half the estimate and its interval excludes zero; else 'throughout') is the app's own convention.
source_note: No literature cited. The doc gives the derivation itself: 'least squares is linear in y, so the two parts' coefficients add up to the primary's'. It is exact: beta = (X'WX)^-1 X'W y is linear in y. The doc's §E23 (line 817-821) explains the choice: the engine has no quantile family, so the split stands in for 'the typical person'. The verdict threshold (more than half, interval excludes zero) has no stated basis.
test_judged: none: no code implements the split (no match for the tail question in turbotab/core or the frontend outside mocks)
note: The additivity is proved by the one-line linearity argument, and the 'mostly the tail' verdict is a labeling convention. Present it as the app's rule. When BE23 is built, add a test that the two coefficients sum to the primary's to machine precision. 'More than half' is ambiguous when the two parts have opposite signs, so the rule should define it, e.g. on the primary's sign. 'From values in the diabetic range' fits the upper part, since only rows above c have nonzero excess. But its coefficient also reflects people moved across the cut, so it is the exposure's association with the excess, not an effect confined to people already diabetic.
